appraisal_events.evidence: "Bonsoir, Monsieur," répondit Charlus, sans même regarder le jeune homme, "d'un air bourru et d'une voix si violemment impolie, que tout le monde en fut stupéfait."
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus greets Mme de Gallardon's nephew with calculated, startling rudeness in front of the whole company, visibly stunning onlookers.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Hé bien, si vous les connaissez, en quoi avez-vous besoin de moi pour vous présenter," me répondit-il d'un ton claquant, et, me tournant le dos.
appraisal_events.explanation: Charlus turns the narrator's own claim of closeness to the Prince against him and curtly rebuffs his request, physically turning away.

appraisal_events.evidence: M. de Bréauté rescues the narrator and presents him to the Prince, whose cold, formal 'Monsieur' the narrator reinterprets: 'je compris tout de suite que l'homme foncièrement dédaigneux était le duc... celui qui était vraiment simple c'était le Prince.'
appraisal_events.explanation: After Bréauté secures the introduction, the narrator concludes the Prince's stiff formality conceals more genuine consideration than the duc's easy camaraderie, which the narrator now reads as fundamentally disdainful.

appraisal_events.evidence: le prince de Guermantes... l'avait aussitôt... entraîné avec lui au fond du jardin, même, dirent certaines personnes, "afin de le mettre à la porte".
appraisal_events.explanation: The Prince abruptly draws Swann away to the back of the garden; some guests interpret this as an expulsion, though the narrator presents this only as rumor, not confirmed fact.

status_effects.explanation: Publicly and visibly humiliated by Charlus's deliberate rudeness in front of the assembled company.
The snub is explicitly witnessed and registered as shocking by 'tout le monde,' marking a public loss of standing.
Both snubs pass without cost to Charlus; the passage notes the Guermantes themselves fear crossing him, underscoring his real social dominance.
Charlus turns the narrator's own words against him, leaving him rebuffed and unable to respond as Charlus walks away.
Through Bréauté's help, the narrator crosses into direct personal acquaintance with the Prince, formally presented and addressed by him.
The narrator's reflection reveals the Prince's apparent haughtiness as concealing more genuine consideration than his cousin's easy charm.
By contrast, the duc's warm familiarity is unmasked by the narrator as concealing a more fundamental disdain.
Swann is abruptly drawn away by the Prince, an act some guests read as an exclusionary expulsion from the gathering, though this is reported as rumor rather than confirmed.

ambiguities: Whether the Prince's removal of Swann was genuinely an expulsion is presented only as rumor ('dirent certaines personnes'), not confirmed by the narrator, which materially lowers confidence in that reading.
